model.label: Tax-funded unified national health system (SUS), free at the point of use and run jointly by federal, state and municipal governments, alongside voluntary private health plans

overview.statement: Brazil's 1988 Constitution made health a universal right and a duty of the state; the unified health system (Sistema Único de Saúde, SUS), created in 1990, is the vehicle for progress towards universal coverage.
Two 1990 laws, 8.080 and 8.142, turned the constitutional right to health into practice and set out how the SUS is organised.

From its start the SUS was meant to be universal, comprehensive and decentralised, and free of charge where services are delivered, resting on principles of equity, solidarity and social participation.

locator.section: Expansion of the Unified Health System in Brazil

overview.statement: Management of the system moved from a centralised social-security bureaucracy to shared (tripartite) governance by municipalities, states and the federal government.

According to the 2024 census of basic health units, most units (85%) are owned by municipalities, but 20% are run under private management arrangements such as social health organisations, charities and other non-profit bodies.

financing.statement: Minimum levels of health spending for each level of government (federal, state and municipal) were introduced in 2000 and written into law in 2012.

locator.section: Expansion of the Unified Health System in Brazil

financing.statement: Between 2003 and 2016 the federal government's share of public health spending fell from 50.0% to 40.8%.
States' share of public health spending rose from 22.3% in 2003 to 27.0% in 2016, and municipalities' share from 25.5% to 32.2%.

A 2018 analysis put public spending at 46.0% of Brazil's health spending, one of the lowest shares in Latin America and the Caribbean (regional average 51.28%) and below the averages for upper-middle-income (55.2%) and OECD (62.2%) countries.

The Constitution makes the private sector complementary to the public one, but in practice the government partly subsidises it through tax breaks for people with private insurance, who also obtain high-complexity procedures in the SUS because their plans cover them poorly or reimburse little.

covered.statement: The SUS runs a national network covering primary, emergency and mental health care, plus specialised centres for transplantation, HIV/AIDS and cancer, supported by a broad pharmaceutical policy.
Expansion of the SUS widened public health programmes such as immunisation, tuberculosis and HIV, and complex services such as organ transplants, cancer care and kidney dialysis.
The national essential medicines list grew from 327 medicines in 2002 to 869 in 2017, alongside policies to improve access to medicines and promote generics.
Since 2011 a national commission (CONITEC) has supported evidence-based decisions on adding new medicines and technologies to the SUS.

A 2026 study of Brazil's health technology assessment system, based on institutional surveys and interviews, found CONITEC widely recognised as central to coordinating evidence and appraisal, but identified possible conflicts of interest and sole reliance on government funding as challenges.
Of 199 drugs added to the SUS after CONITEC appraisal between 2012 and 2024, 64 were projected to save money, with projected savings of Int$6.67 billion.

Family health teams were originally made up of a general practitioner, a nurse, a nursing technician or assistant and four to six community health workers, each worker making routine home visits to around 150 families in a small area.

locator.section: The transformation of the Family Health Program into a strategy

cost_sharing.statement: Since 2004 the Popular Pharmacy Programme (Farmácia Popular) has widened access to medicines at subsidised prices with low copayments.
Out-of-pocket payments, though reduced, made up nearly half of private health spending in this 2018 analysis and remained a considerable burden for households.
In the 2017/18 household budget survey, medicines were the largest part of out-of-pocket health spending, reaching 85% of such payments among the lowest consumption deciles.
Catastrophic health spending has declined since 2004, but medicines remain an important item in the budgets of the poorest families.

financial_hardship.statement: Using the 2017/18 national household budget survey, World Bank researchers estimated that over 10 million Brazilians a year are pushed into poverty by out-of-pocket health payments, 4.87% of people, compared with 2.5% globally and 1.8% in Latin America and the Caribbean.
The same study found that a third of households spent more than 10% of their budget on health, and that financial hardship was much more common among the poor (37% in the bottom consumption deciles).

additional_care.statement: In 2019, 59.7 million people (28.5% of residents) had a private medical or dental health plan, not significantly different from 27.9% in 2013.

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: Plan coverage in 2019 was highest in the Southeast (37.5%), South (32.8%) and Centre-West (28.9%) and lowest in the North (14.7%) and Northeast (16.6%).

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: In 2019 only 2.2% of people with household income per person of up to a quarter of the minimum wage had a medical plan, compared with 86.8% of those with more than five minimum wages a month.

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: Dental plans were much less common than medical plans in 2019: 12.9% of people had a dental plan and 26.0% a medical plan.

locator.section: Cobertura de plano de saúde, médico ou odontológico

additional_care.statement: Private medical insurance grew from 30.5 million people (17.6%) in 2000 to 50.3 million (24.8%) in 2014, then fell to 47.3 million (22.8%) in 2017 as incomes and employment declined.

Private health plans must pay the SUS back when their members are treated in the public system; the 2025 Agora Tem Especialistas law lets plan operators settle these debts by providing free care instead.

access.statement: In 2019 the public basic health unit (Unidade Básica de Saúde) was the place people most often said they usually went for care (46.8%), ahead of private practices or clinics (22.9%) and public emergency units or hospital emergency departments (14.1%).

locator.section: Acesso e utilização dos serviços de saúde

access.statement: In 2019, 76.2% of people (159.6 million) had seen a doctor in the previous 12 months, up from 71.2% in 2013.

locator.section: Acesso e utilização dos serviços de saúde

access.statement: In 2019, 60.0% of households (44.0 million) were registered with a family health unit, up from 53.3% in 2013.
Of people hospitalised for 24 hours or more in the year before the 2019 survey, 64.6% (8.9 million) were admitted through the SUS.

Reliance on the SUS for hospital care falls steeply with income: in 2019 the last hospital stay was through the SUS for 95.0% of hospitalised people with household income per person of up to a quarter of the minimum wage, but for only 6.8% of those with more than five minimum wages.

Brazil has almost doubled its medical workforce since 2003, to 2.77 doctors per 1,000 people, with the largest increase after the 2013 More Doctors legislation; poorer, remote states gained, but most new doctors and students are still in richer regions.
Doctor shortages persist in rural areas and in primary care, and specialists are concentrated in the private sector and unevenly spread across the country.
Ministry of Health data from 2025 show a shortage and uneven distribution of medical specialists, who are concentrated in the private network and in the Southeast region.

outcomes.statement: Infant mortality fell from 53.4 to 12.7 deaths per 1,000 live births between 1990 and 2023, life expectancy rose from 65 years in 1985 to 76.8 years in 2025, and polio (1989) and measles (2000) were eliminated.
In the GBD 2019 study, Brazil's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 53.0 (95% uncertainty interval 51.5-54.3) in 2019, 17.5 points higher than in 1990.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location, 2019 overall (0-74 years) and absolute change 1990-2019 overall

outcomes.statement: By age group in the GBD 2019 study, Brazil's 2019 HAQ Index score was 62.4 for ages 0-14, 53.4 for ages 15-64 and 48.6 for ages 65-74.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location, 2019, young (0-14), working (15-64) and post-working (65-74) age groups

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2016 HAQ Index, Brazil was in the sixth of ten deciles nationally; the Federal District reached the eighth decile (score 75.4), while most states, especially northern ones, were in the fifth.
The gap in HAQ Index scores between Brazil's states widened slightly, from 17.2 points in 1990 to 20.4 points in 2016, although Brazil's overall progress was steadier over time than Mexico's.
A study of all Brazilian microregions in 2008-2017 found no significant effect of the extra primary care doctors supplied by the Mais Médicos programme on hospitalisation or mortality rates.

After Cuban doctors left the More Doctors programme, affected municipalities saw lasting falls in chronic-disease care, while use of urgent services such as maternal care and infection treatment soon recovered; the fall in use did not translate into changes in health outcomes.

costs.statement: Total health spending rose from 7.0% to 8.3% of GDP between 2000 and 2014, and per-person spending from US$263 to US$947.
Municipal health spending per person grew 226% in real terms between 2003 and 2014 (from R$315.7 to R$716.5), then fell 6.3% to R$617.1 in 2016.
Most of the federal budget goes to debt service, which rose from 50.3% of the budget in 2013 to 57.0% in 2016, limiting fiscal space for other areas such as health.

For drugs paid for solely by the Ministry of Health, the projected added budget impact of CONITEC-approved drugs equalled 29% of the specialised pharmaceutical care budget in 2024, and over 45% in 2019-2022.
In 2019, court-ordered purchases took 25.2% of the federal budget for the Specialised Component of Pharmaceutical Care, with 21% going to 10 medicines.

what_works.statement: A 2019 review of the SUS's first 30 years concluded that Brazil, despite successes and setbacks, has reached nearly universal access to health-care services.
The Family Health Strategy's population coverage rose from 13.2 million people (7.8%) in 2000 to 120.2 million (58.5%) in 2016.

Between 2002 and 2013, as the SUS expanded, access to essential services such as immunisation and antenatal care became nearly universal, population health improved and regional health inequalities declined.

locator.section: Expansion of the Unified Health System in Brazil

what_works.statement: Family health coverage is concentrated where it is most needed: in the 2019 national health survey it reached 74% of the poorest income fifth against 38% of the richest, and people registered with it more often had a regular source of care (79% vs 73%).

locator.section: Impact of the expansion of FHS coverage on access and population health

what_works.statement: Studies, mostly longitudinal ecological analyses, link the Family Health Strategy to lower infant and under-5 mortality and fewer avoidable hospital admissions among adults and older people, with larger effects in vulnerable groups.

locator.section: Impact of the expansion of FHS coverage on access and population health

what_works.statement: Medical students became more diverse after the 2013 More Doctors legislation: women rose from 55.5% of students in 2013 to 61.4% in 2023 and mixed-race students from 19.4% to 25.5%, though most students remain white and from fee-paying secondary schools.

A 13-year review found CONITEC's drug coverage decisions consistent with affordability principles, judged on the projections available at decision time rather than on real-world spending after adoption.
When many doctors left suddenly, the system adapted: more supply from elsewhere and patients seeking care in other places helped avoid major harm to population health at the market level.

problems.statement: A 2018 analysis found persistent structural problems in the SUS, including weak organisation and governance, low public funding and poor resource allocation, leaving large regional gaps in access and outcomes that hit poorer regions and groups hardest.

Chronic underfunding, made worse by the 2016 spending cap, limits the system, and specialised services, intensive care beds and diagnostic equipment are concentrated in wealthier regions and in the private sector.
Waiting lists for surgery, biopsies and radiotherapy are long and still growing, and the cancer care network has not kept pace with the rising cancer burden.
Maternal mortality remains high for Brazil's level of development, and the health workforce is unevenly distributed because strategies to attract, retain and train staff across regions fall short.
Shortages of some specialist services and weak administrative capacity have produced poor-quality hospital services with long waits.

Courts help secure access when the state fails to supply medicines already in the SUS, but orders to buy medicines not incorporated into the system compromise access to medicines for the wider population.
Among households registered with a family health unit for at least a year, 38.4% had a monthly visit from a community health worker or team member in 2019, down from 47.2% in 2013.

About 23.8% (9.5 million) of households registered with a family health unit for at least a year had never been visited by a community health worker or team member in 2019, up from 17.7% (5.3 million) in 2013.

Under the Previne Brasil financing model, only one of seven primary care performance indicators (syphilis and HIV testing in pregnancy: 62.5% against a 60% target) met its target on average from early 2022 to early 2023.
Student achievement scores and resources show significantly lower teaching quality in private medical schools, which drove much of the expansion.
The authors conclude that, despite universal coverage, financial protection is not yet guaranteed, especially for the poor, and that better access to affordable essential medicines is key.

reforms.statement: On 7 October 2025 the President signed Law 15.233/25, which grew out of a provisional measure (MP 1301/25) the federal government issued on 30 May.

Law 15.233/2025 creates the Agora Tem Especialistas programme, joined by private hospitals (for-profit or not), to expand beds and services and cut waiting times for specialist consultations, procedures and tests in the SUS.

The programme has three main parts: federal tax credits for private hospitals and clinics that join, letting private plans swap their debts to the SUS for care provided, and direct specialist care by the federal government in emergencies the Ministry recognises.
Total federal tax benefits under Agora Tem Especialistas are capped at R$2 billion a year.

A 2026 analysis argued that Agora Tem Especialistas should not be seen as privatising the universal system, since it does not raise private health spending, expand private plans or hand public responsibilities to the private sector, but said its effect on regional and public-private inequalities must be monitored.

The national primary care quality improvement programme (PMAQ-AB) was wound down from 2017 and ended in 2019, replaced by Previne Brasil, which relied on a narrow set of process indicators and was itself discontinued in 2024.
A study of Pernambuco's municipalities in 2018-2024 found that the federal government's share of primary care funding was larger after Previne Brasil was discontinued.

From 2019 to 2023, Previne Brasil replaced funding based on the whole catchment population with funding by individually registered patients, which the authors say limited collective action, restricted access to registered patients and undermined universality, comprehensiveness and equity.

In 2023, as family health was made a priority again, the federal support teams (NASF) were reformed into federally co-financed multidisciplinary primary care teams with a wider remit, including telehealth.

The More Doctors for Brazil project was relaunched in 2023, emphasising rebuilding teams, training and retaining doctors in priority areas, after the 2019 Doctors for Brazil programme was slow to start and limited in reach.
A 2023 provisional measure (MP 1,165/2023) revived More Doctors with 15,000 new vacancies.

Constitutional Amendment 126/2022 abolished the 2016 expenditure ceiling, which had in practice frozen real federal primary spending for 20 years, and opened R$145 billion of extra room in the 2023 budget.

The replacement fiscal rule proposed in 2023 (the New Sustainable Fiscal Regime, PLP 93/2023, still before the Senate when this editorial was written) caps real growth in federal spending at 70% of real revenue growth and at most 2.5% a year.

At the end of 2018, after the elections, Cuba ended its PAHO-mediated agreement and withdrew most Cuban doctors; the Bolsonaro government then launched Médicos pelo Brasil, which required doctors trained abroad to validate their diplomas in Brazil.

Constitutional Amendment 95, passed in December 2016, limited federal primary spending on health for 20 years: 15% of net current revenue in 2017 and then 2017 levels adjusted for inflation, with a projected decline of R$415 billion in the health budget by 2036 as described in 2018 (the ceiling has since been abolished; see the Amendment 126/2022 entry).
In 2013 the Rousseff government launched the More Doctors (Mais Médicos) programme, sending more than 18,000 doctors, mostly from Cuba, to underserved areas to expand primary care.
